sec.title: Question
sec.p: Does adding the immune checkpoint inhibitor avelumab to first-line methotrexate improve cure rates in low-risk gestational trophoblastic tumors (GTT)?

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: In this phase 1/2 nonrandomized clinical trial of 26 patients, the addition of avelumab to first-line methotrexate demonstrated a manageable safety profile and resulted in human chorionic gonadotropin normalization with treatment discontinuation and no relapse in 96.2% of patients after a median of 41 months of follow-up. Among patients interested in pregnancy, 93% subsequently conceived, suggesting preserved fertility.

sec.title: Meaning
sec.p: Avelumab plus methotrexate may represent a promising first-line option for low-risk GTT, with potential to reduce methotrexate resistance, particularly in patients with higher International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics scores.

sec.title: Importance
sec.p: Low-risk gestational trophoblastic tumors (GTT; International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics [FIGO] score ≤6) are typically treated with single-agent chemotherapy, achieving cure rates of approximately 70%. Avelumab (anti–programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 monoclonal antibody) has demonstrated activity in chemotherapy-resistant GTT, supporting investigation in earlier treatment settings.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of avelumab combined with methotrexate as first-line therapy in patients with low-risk GTT.

sec.title: Design, Setting, and Participants
sec.p: TROPHAMET (Avelumab and Methotrexate in Low-Risk Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasias as First-Line Treatment) was a multicenter, phase 1/2 nonrandomized clinical trial of patients with low-risk GTT (FIGO score ≤6) treated at academic referral centers. The study period was from April 14, 2020, to December 5, 2023, with a follow-up of 41 months. Data were analyzed from December 20, 2024, to July 3, 2025.

sec.title: Interventions
sec.p: Avelumab, 800 mg, intravenously on day 1 plus methotrexate, 1 mg/kg, intramuscularly on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 alternating with oral folinic acid in 2-week cycles until normalization of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) level; and followed by 3 consolidation cycles.

sec.title: Main Outcomes and Measures
sec.p: Phase 1 primary end point was dose-limiting toxic effects (DLTs); phase 2 primary end point was the rate of serum hCG normalization permitting treatment discontinuation.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Of 27 female patients treated (median [range] age, 35 [20-50] years), 26 were assessable for efficacy. Eight patients (31%) had FIGO scores of 1 to 2; 8 patients (31%) had scores of 3 to 4; and 10 patients (38%) had scores of 5 to 6. The treatment regimen demonstrated acceptable safety: 1 DLT occurred (grade 3 sepsis on central venous catheter); immune- and treatment-related adverse events of grade 2 or higher occurred in 6 patients (22%), all of which fully resolved except for 1 case of grade 2 dysthyroidism; and there were no grade 4 or higher events. The rate of successful hCG normalization was 96.2% (90% CI, 85.9%-97.9%). After a median (IQR) follow-up of 41 (37-45) months, no relapses were observed. Among patients with childbearing potential and pregnancy intention, 13 of 14 achieved pregnancy (93%).

sec.title: Conclusions and Relevance
sec.p: In this nonrandomized clinical trial, avelumab combined with methotrexate demonstrated a manageable safety profile and high efficacy in low-risk GTT in more than 95% of patients, with durable responses and preserved fertility. This combination may represent a promising first-line strategy warranting evaluation in comparative studies, particularly for patients at higher risk of chemoresistance.

sec.p: Received 2026 Feb 18; Accepted 2026 Apr 16.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Low-risk gestational trophoblastic tumors (GTT) have an International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) 2000 risk score of 6 or less and represent approximately 80% of malignant gestational trophoblastic disease forms. Standard treatment for patients with low-risk GTT is single-agent chemotherapy, most commonly with actinomycin-D or the 8-day methotrexate protocol (modified by Bagshawe et al). Treatment with methotrexate is continued until either normalization of serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) concentration (followed by 2-3 consolidation cycles) or resistance is detected. Reported rates of hCG normalization with methotrexate vary widely in the literature, ranging from 54% to 90%, reflecting substantial heterogeneity across studies, mainly from retrospective analyses of clinical data. In particular, it has been reported that normalization rates decrease with increasing FIGO risk scores. Overall, methotrexate induces hCG normalization in approximately 70% of patients with low-risk GTT. In the case of resistance to methotrexate, subsequent treatment options include actinomycin D, which is associated with a cure rate of approximately 75%, and EMA-CO regimens (etoposide, methotrexate, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide, and vincristine), which have a 100% cure rate but a higher risk of acute and long-term toxic effects.

There is strong biological rationale for immunotherapy activity in GTT. Cases of spontaneous regression of metastatic disease have been reported, suggesting that the immune system plays an important role in GTT development and progression. Programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) is also constitutively expressed in all premalignant and malignant trophoblast subtypes. Pembrolizumab (anti–programmed cell death 1 protein [PD-1]) has demonstrated activity in case reports of chemotherapy-resistant GTT. In prospective studies, camrelizumab (anti−PD-1) plus apatinib achieved hCG normalization in 50% of patients with polychemotherapy-resistant disease. In the TROPHIMMUN trial cohort A, avelumab (anti–PD-L1) produced an hCG normalization rate of 53% in patients resistant to single-agent chemotherapy, with no relapses after 4 years of follow-up—consistent with achieving long-term disease-free recovery. Notably, at least 33% of these patients avoided the need for toxic polychemotherapy.

We hypothesized that adding avelumab to methotrexate as first-line treatment for low-risk GTT could increase efficacy, and therefore, the probability of disease recovery, reducing the need for subsequent treatments. This study sought to report safety and activity results from the TROPHAMET phase 1/2 nonrandomized clinical trial investigating avelumab plus methotrexate use in patients with low-risk GTT.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The trial protocol was approved by the French national health authorities (Agence nationale de sécurité du médicament et des produits de santé) and French independent ethics committee (Comité de Protection des personnes). Patients were enrolled per international standards of good clinical practice and institutional safety monitoring. All patients provided written informed consent before trial enrollment. The full trial protocol, along with protocol amendment details, are provided in Supplement 1. We followed the Enhancing Reporting Quality and Impact of Early Phase Dose-Finding Clinical Trials: CONSORT Dose-Finding Extension (CONSORT-DEFINE) guidelines.

sec.title: Trial Design
sec.p: TROPHAMET (Avelumab and Methotrexate in Low-Risk Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasias as First-Line Treatment) was an investigator-initiated, open-label, phase 1/2 nonrandomized clinical trial of avelumab plus methotrexate in patients with low-risk GTT. The trial was sponsored by Hospices Civils de Lyon (France) and was conducted across 9 centers that are part of the French Gestational Trophoblastic Center network (Centre de Reference des Maladies Trophoblastiques, Lyon, France) and specialized in early phase trials. TROPHAMET included a safety run-in phase 1 part to confirm safety in 6 patients, followed by a phase 2 part to assess efficacy.

sec.title: Trial Participants
sec.p: Eligible patients were adult women (age ≥18 years) with low-risk GTT (FIGO score ≤6) who had a medical indication of methotrexate as first-line treatment from April 14, 2020, to December 5, 2023, with a follow-up of 41 months. Additional eligibility criteria included Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 2 or less; adequate bone marrow, kidney, and hepatic functions; and no contraindications to immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment. Patients were excluded if they had received prior immunotherapy.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: Baseline assessments of participants included thoracic, abdominal, pelvic, and brain contrast-enhanced imaging; left ventricular ejection fraction assessment; archival curettage or tumoral tissue biopsy; patient interview and clinical examination, including electrocardiogram; and standard blood and/or urine assessments. Regarding lung metastatic involvement, FIGO disease stage was defined based on thoracic computed tomography scan findings but the FIGO score calculation was based on visible lesions on chest radiography imaging, as per the Practical Guidelines for the Treatment of Gestational Trophoblastic Disease.

Patients received 2-week cycles of the standard 8-day methotrexate regimen (1 mg/kg via intramuscular injection on days 1, 3, 5, and 7, alternating with oral folinic acid 10 mg/d) plus avelumab (800 mg flat-dose intravenously) administered before methotrexate on day 1. Treatment continued until the institutional normal serum hCG concentration was reached, followed by 3 consolidation cycles; hCG resistance occurred (>20% rise in hCG from baseline maintained for 3 consecutive weekly assessments or hCG plateau with <10% decrease in 3 of 4 consecutive weekly assessments); unacceptable toxic effects and/or death; intercurrent illness that prevented further treatment; or patient withdrawal (Figure 1).

sec.p: Safety was assessed every 2 weeks during cycles 1 to 4 and then every 2 cycles thereafter. Adverse events (AEs) were classified according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5.0 (US National Cancer Institute). Serum hCG levels were measured every week at the patient laboratory and confirmed at the hospital where the patient was treated. Following discontinuation after either hCG normalization or resistance, baseline imaging assessments were repeated 1 month after the last treatment cycle. Subsequent follow-up was ensured by the French Gestational Trophoblastic Center up to 3 years after hCG normalization according to French procedures for low-risk patients (Figure 1). Subsequent hCG rises were investigated to differentiate a relapse or new pregnancy.

sec.title: Primary and Secondary Outcomes
sec.p: The primary end point in the safety run-in phase 1 part was dose-limiting toxic effects (DLTs). DLT are detailed in Supplement 2. In phase 1, 6 patients were to be enrolled in 2 subsequent cohorts of 3 patients and monitored by the data and safety monitoring board, to confirm that fewer than 1 of 3 patients had DLT in each cohort. If of 2 or fewer of 6 patients had a DLT, recruitment would continue to phase 2.

The primary end point in phase 2 was the percentage of patients with hCG normalization that led to treatment discontinuation without the need for subsequent treatment. Patients assessable for efficacy had received 2 or more cycles of trial treatment, whereas patients assessable for safety had received 1 or more treatment dose. The trial had a 2-step design following the Simon minimax design (1-sided 5% α risk and 80% power). Treatment would not be considered effective if the success rate (hCG normalization) was 70% or less; a success rate of 90% was expected. To reject the null hypothesis, enrollment of 26 efficacy-assessable patients was planned, with 23 enrolled in the first stage. If 19 or fewer of 23 successes were observed, enrollment would stop due to lack of efficacy. If 20 or more successes were observed, enrollment would continue up to 26 patients. If 22 or more of 26 successes were observed, the trial would be considered positive.

Secondary end points included safety (treatment-related AEs [TRAEs] and immune-related TRAEs), overall survival, and time to relapse (time from trial inclusion to observation of relapse). Relapse was defined as a rise in hCG after normalization and treatment discontinuation that required subsequent treatment. Additional exploratory analyses were performed of hCG normalization rates according to disease stage, FIGO score, concomitant use (≥1 dose) of medications that could potentially alter immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy (eg, steroids, antihistamines, antibiotics), and subsequent fertility in patients with child-bearing potential who did not present with disease relapse after a minimum of 1 year of follow-up after treatment discontinuation (eg, interest in conception, pregnancy rate, and outcomes).

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed from December 20, 2024, to July 3, 2025, using SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc). Tests were 1-tailed and significance was defined as P < .05.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between April 14, 2020, and December 5, 2023, we enrolled 29 patients of whom 2 withdrew from the trial before receiving any treatment (1 spontaneous hCG decline after consent and 1 patient decision). Additionally, 1 patient withdrew following 1 treatment cycle because she developed grade 2 immune-related colitis. Therefore, 27 patients (median [range] age, 35 [20-50] years), were assessable for safety, and 26 for efficacy (Figure 2). Overall, 8 patients were enrolled in the safety run-in phase 1 part. Initially, 6 patients were enrolled, per protocol, but 2 developed grade 2 immune-related colitis (confirmed by colonoscopy) after 8 and 18 days of treatment, respectively, which fully resolved after avelumab discontinuation. Both patients were found to have a family history of autoimmune disorders, leading to a protocol amendment to exclude patients with a first-degree relative family autoimmune disorder history. Per protocol, these AEs were not defined as DLTs; however, because these patients discontinued avelumab in the DLT observation period, an additional 2 patients were enrolled. Subsequently 21 patients were enrolled in the phase 2 part (18 and 3 in the first and second steps, respectively).

sec.p: Among the 26 patients assessable for efficacy, median (range) age was 34.5 (20-50) years and the FIGO score was 5 to 6 in 10 patients (38%; Table 1). The details of FIGO score items are shown in eTable 1 in Supplement 2. More than half of patients (14 [54%]) had stage III disease with lung metastases. Per the last pathology samples obtained, 24 patients (92%) had an antecedent of complete mole on curettage specimens. Among 5 patients older than 42 years, 2 patients had persisting high hCG despite previous hysterectomy, and the remaining 3 patients had lung metastases justifying systemic treatment.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: During the safety run-in phase 1 period, 1 patient had grade 3 sepsis associated with a central venous catheter infection without neutropenia during her fourth treatment cycle, which was assessed as a DLT. This event was fully resolved with antibiotics and ablation of the catheter.

In all 27 patients assessable for safety, discontinuation and/or dose modification of methotrexate and/or avelumab occurred in 5 patients (19%). One patient discontinued avelumab after 1 cycle due to grade 2 immune-related colitis and withdrew from the trial. One patient discontinued avelumab after 2 cycles due to grade 2 immune-related colitis, and then methotrexate after 3 cycles due to grade 2 mucositis and grade 2 hand-foot syndrome. Another patient discontinued avelumab after 2 cycles and had a 25% methotrexate dose reduction from cycle 2 onwards due to grade 2 liver toxicity (elevated aspartate and alanine aminotransferase levels) that subsequently resolved. Two additional patients had methotrexate dose reductions: 1 patient had a 25% reduction from cycle 2 onwards due to grade 3 mucositis and the other patient had a 20% reduction for cycle 6 and 7, followed by an additional reduction to 55% from cycle 8 onwards due to grade 2 liver toxicity.

Overall, any-grade TRAEs occurred in 25 patients (93%; Table 2). The most common any-grade TRAEs (≥20% of patients) were those frequently observed with methotrexate, including mucositis (16 patients [59%]), nausea (10 [37%]), and asthenia (9 [33%]). Grade 3 TRAEs occurred in 5 patients (19%): mucositis (stomatitis) in 2 patients (7%, including 1 patient who did not take folinic acid due to a local pharmaceutical dispensation error), liver toxicity in 2 patients (7%), and sepsis in 1 patient (4%, DLT described above); no grade 4 or 5 TRAEs occurred. Six patients (22%) had a grade 2 or higher immune-related TRAE (Table 2). Two patients (7%) had a grade 3 liver toxicity (methotrexate-related per investigators), and 1 patient (4%) had a grade 2 liver toxicity (avelumab-related per investigator). As previously described, 2 patients (7%) had grade 2 immune-related colitis, of whom 1 (4%) also had grade 2 arthritis (4%). One patient (4%) had grade 2 hyperthyroidism followed by grade 2 hypothyroidism.

sec.p: All immune-related TRAEs fully resolved except for the hypothyroidism in 1 patient. Steroids were administered for immune-related TRAEs in 4 patients.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: In 26 patients assessable for efficacy, median (range) number of avelumab cycles was 8 (2-21), and methotrexate cycles was 8 (3-21). A successful hCG normalization occurred in 25 patients (96.2%; 90% CI, 85.9%-97.9%; Figure 3). Median (IQR) time to normalization was 3.4 (2.5-4.1) months. Rates of hCG normalization were similar across subgroups based on disease stage, FIGO score, and concomitant treatments of interest (eTable 2 in Supplement 2).

sec.p: At data cutoff, median (IQR) follow-up was 41 (37-45) months. No patient with hCG normalization had relapsed after discontinuing treatment, consistent with disease recovery. The relapse-free survival rate was 100% and the 36-month overall survival rate was 100%. One patient with a FIGO score of 5 developed treatment resistance (hCG increase) after 16 cycles of combination treatment. She was subsequently treated with the etoposide-methotrexate-actinomycin D-cyclophosphamide-oncovin (EMA-CO) regimen to which her disease was also resistant. Finally, she was successfully treated with a combination of hysterectomy and platinum-based chemotherapy (paclitaxel-etoposide alternating with paclitaxel-cisplatin regimen).

sec.title: Subsequent Fertility
sec.p: Patients were deemed to have child-bearing potential if they had hCG normalization, a 1 year or longer of follow-up after normalization without relapse, were younger than 42 years, at data collection, and had not had a hysterectomy. Overall, 21 patients had child-bearing potential, of whom 14 wanted to conceive. After a median follow-up of 33 months, 13 of 14 patients (93%) became pregnant, all within 19 months of attempting conception. As of February 1, 2026, 1 patient chose a voluntary termination of pregnancy; and among the remaining 12 patients, 10 (83%) delivered a healthy infant, and 2 (17%) experienced involuntary termination (ie, miscarriage).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: To our knowledge, TROPHAMET is the first prospective trial of an immunotherapy combined with methotrexate as first-line treatment for patients with low-risk GTT. No new safety concerns were observed with this combination treatment, and 96.2% of patients achieved hCG normalization. Collectively, these findings support TROPHAMET and are proof-of-concept that adding an immune checkpoint inhibitor to standard chemotherapy may reduce the risk of chemoresistance.

Avelumab plus methotrexate demonstrated a manageable safety profile, with 22% of patients experiencing grade 2 or higher immune-related TRAEs. Two patients with immune-related colitis were subsequently found to have a family history of autoimmune disorders, leading to a protocol amendment excluding patients with a first-degree family history of autoimmune disease. Applying this criterion would reduce the incidence of immune-related TRAEs to approximately 15%. Grade 2 or 3 hepatotoxicity was observed in 11 patients (41%), appearing higher than reported in the only prospective study of methotrexate alone (>53% for all grade, and >13% for grade ≥2 in a Chinese population), although the attributable risk remains uncertain given the limited prospective data. Among these, liver enzyme elevations were considered treatment-related in 3 patients—attributed to methotrexate in 2 patients and to avelumab in 1 patient—highlighting the difficulty in determining causality without histologic assessment. Overall, immune-related toxic effects resolved without sequelae, except for grade 2 hypothyroidism in 1 patient (4%).

At last follow-up (median 41 months), no relapses had occurred, indicating that patients likely recovered given that most GTT relapses occur within 12 months. These results would indicate that more than 95% of patients were successfully treated with this combination. This rate appears numerically higher than the 54% to 90% range of long-term hCG normalization reported with the 8-day methotrexate regimen, acknowledging that the 2 main prospective trials reported normalization rates of 54% in China and 88% among Western populations. Efficacy outcomes were particularly promising in patients with FIGO scores of 4 to 6 or 5 to 6, with cure rates of 92% and 90%, respectively—numerically exceeding the less than 50% success rates reported by Sita-Lumsden et al.

Additionally, during follow-up, 93% of patients with child-bearing potential and intention subsequently became pregnant, 83% of whom had healthy pregnancies and deliveries, and 17% were still ongoing, providing reassurance regarding the lack of impact on fertility. The observed miscarriage rate (17%) was consistent with the 8% to 24% range reported in the literature after single-agent chemotherapy for low-risk GTT.

Only 1 patient had resistance to the combination treatment. This patient was also highly resistant to all subsequent combination chemotherapy regimens received. Translational research to identify biomarkers of resistance is ongoing. A retrospective analysis of TROPHIMMUN trial suggested that patients with high-affinity Fc γ R3A (CD16) homozygous polymorphism were more likely to recover with avelumab treatment in situations of chemoresistance, as a result of increased activation of natural killer cells through antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity. Similar analyses are planned for samples taken from patients in TROPHAMET. Of note, PD-L1 expression was not assessed because there is no definitive evidence significantly associating expression with efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors in GTT.

These results raise the question of whether a methotrexate plus avelumab regimen would be appropriate for all patients with low-risk disease. Beyond the increased toxic effects associated with immune-related adverse events, it remains uncertain whether the additional cost of adding avelumab to first-line methotrexate would be offset by a reduced risk of chemoresistance and its associated health care expenditures. Indeed, fewer patients would require subsequent lines of single-agent chemotherapy (actinomycin-D) or combination chemotherapy regimens, such as EMA-CO, that are associated with repeated hospitalizations for toxic effects management, work absences, patient and family anxiety regarding resistance and toxicity, and potential long-term toxic effects. Therefore, cost-effectiveness, patient preference, and quality-of-life analyses of this combination are warranted, particularly in patients at higher risk of methotrexate resistance (FIGO score, 4-6), to inform decision-making by health authorities, stakeholders, and patients.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This trial had limitations, including its single-arm, open-label phase 2 design. The number of patients was small (N = 27), limiting the power of these analyses; however, GTT is a rare cancer, and most historical data are from retrospective and observational studies, without assessment of success rates. To our knowledge, TROPHAMET is the third prospective trial of an immunotherapy in patients with GTT, following TROPHIMMUN and a phase 2 trial of camrelizumab plus apatinib, both in later treatment lines. Moreover, the feasibility of a randomized phase 3 trial in this population is uncertain, as shown by the early termination because of insufficient recruitment of a phase 3 trial comparing actinomycin-D vs 8-day methotrexate in patients with low-risk GTT. More recently, a randomized phase 2 trial comparing these same regimens was reported in a cohort of patients in China with very low-risk GTT (FIGO score 0-4) with 54% chance of hCG normalization. In TROPHAMET, the absence of centralized hCG measurements may have reduced the accuracy of assessing hCG kinetics because of variability among the assays used. However, the hCG value of on day 1 of each cycle was confirmed locally at the treating hospital to mitigate this heterogeneity (Figure 1).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The TROPHAMET nonrandomized clinical trial, a proof-of-concept trial, demonstrates that the addition of avelumab to methotrexate may reduce the risk of resistance to methotrexate and successfully treat more than 95% of patients with low-risk GTT in the first-line setting. In the context of the limited evidence available for this rare disease, this regimen was observed to be highly effective in a prospective study and may inform future treatment strategies for patients with low-risk GTT. Larger prospective studies are needed to confirm efficacy, evaluate the safety and cost-effectiveness of anti−PD-L1/anti−PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors, and determine whether the benefit applies to the overall low-risk population or specific patient subgroups, with the broader objective of further improving cure rates in low-risk GTT.
